opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to acknowledge is that simulators will never fully capture the richness of the real world. The world has an enormous long tail: different terrains, materials, lighting, friction, objects with all kinds of shapes and deformations. If you try to hand-engineer all of that into a simulator, you will always fall short.

So my view is that we shouldn't try to make the simulator perfect. Instead, we should use it for what it's good at: giving us lots of cheap, safe experience to learn the basic skills, the "motor babbling" if you like. Then we deal with the gap in two ways.

One is randomization. You vary the parameters of the simulation widely, masses, frictions, terrain profiles, delays, so the policy doesn't overfit to one particular version of physics. It learns to be robust across a whole family of worlds, and hopefully the real world sits somewhere inside that family.

The second, and to me the more interesting one, is adaptation. Biological creatures don't have a perfect model of the world either. A child walking on sand for the first time adjusts within a few steps. So we want robots that, at deployment, can infer from their own recent history of sensations and actions what kind of environment they're in, and adjust their behavior online. You train in simulation to be an adaptive agent, not just a fixed controller.

And finally, I'd say simulation shouldn't be the only source of data. There's an enormous amount of video of humans interacting with the world, and the robot's own real-world experience. Combining simulation for the basics with real-world data for the diversity is, I think, the way forward. The simulator is a starting point, not the destination.

r002.rationale: It does not compare simulation and real-world testing to a scientific theory-and-experiment cycle.

r003.rationale: It does not mention building environments from scans or capturing real-world statistical properties.

r004.rationale: It makes no reference to Hollywood graphics or physical effects as evidence for robot simulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's important to first recognize that simulation has been enormously valuable, especially for things like locomotion. We've seen that for legged robots, you can train policies entirely in simulation and transfer them to the real world, and the reason that works is that the physics of a body with a dozen joints interacting with terrain is something we can model reasonably well. The gap there is about contact dynamics and motor properties, and you can bridge it with domain randomization and with the robot adapting online from its own proprioceptive history.

But when you move to manipulation, or really to anything where vision is central, the diversity problem becomes much more severe. The real world has an essentially unbounded variety of objects, materials, lighting conditions, clutter. No simulator is going to enumerate all of that. So I don't think the answer is to make the simulator perfect. I think there are a few complementary directions.

One is to be deliberately modest about what you ask simulation to do. Use it for the parts of the problem where physics is well understood, like whole-body control and dynamics, and don't pretend it's going to teach the robot what every kitchen in the world looks like.

The second is to lean on the enormous amount of real-world visual data that already exists. Humans have put billions of images and videos online, and the progress in computer vision over the last decade comes from learning representations from that data. A robot's visual system should inherit those representations rather than being trained from scratch in a rendered environment. The simulator then only has to handle the part that's genuinely about the robot's body and its actions.

The third is procedural generation and generative models. Instead of a human artist building a few hundred scenes, you can have systems that generate enormous numbers of plausible environments, and increasingly you can use learned generative models to produce visual variety that approximates the statistics of the real world.

And finally, I think we should take inspiration from how children learn. A child doesn't experience a billion random environments either. The child has a relatively small amount of experience but learns in a structured, developmental way, building up abstractions that generalize. So part of the answer isn't more diversity in simulation. It's building learning systems that extract the right invariances from limited experience, so they don't need to have seen everything in advance. Sim-to-real is as much a question about representation and adaptation as it is about how rich the simulator is.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to have a loop between simulation and the real world. A simulator captures some of the variation, but inevitably it leaves things out. You can vary the objects, the lighting, the friction, and so on, but you’re still varying things within a model that you have chosen.

So you have to take the robot into the real world and see where it fails. Those failures tell you what is missing from your simulator. You improve the simulator, train again, and repeat. And some learning will have to happen through real interaction, because you cannot anticipate every situation.

The goal should be to make simulation useful for learning, rather than to expect it to reproduce the entire richness of the world.

r003.rationale: It does not mention building simulation environments from scans of real spaces or capturing real-world statistical properties.

r004.rationale: It does not cite Hollywood graphics or physical effects as evidence for robot simulation prospects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should be careful about expecting a simulator to capture all the diversity of the real world. You can vary the objects, the lighting, the materials, the physics, and that certainly helps. But those variations still reflect what somebody thought to put into the simulator. The real world will surprise you.

So I would think of simulation as a place to learn useful things and get started, with real-world experience providing the correction. The robot needs to encounter situations where its assumptions fail, and then learn from those failures. You can use those experiences to improve the simulator as well. It becomes a loop between simulation and reality, rather than a requirement that we build a perfect simulated world before the robot can do anything.
